# RHO: Your Coding Agent is Secretly a Roboticist

> RHO searches multi-file robot policy repositories before deployment. Explore held-out generalization, deployment latency, real robot trials, and the cost of search.

- **Authors**: Anonymous

## Abstract

Code-as-Policies (CaP) has shown that large language models (LLMs) can write code to solve robotics tasks by composing perception, planning, and control primitives. Recent CaP systems, however, rely on multi-turn code-generation loops at test time, which is often infeasible for real-time robot control. We introduce **Robotics Harness Optimization (RHO)**, a novel paradigm in which tool-enabled coding agents, *at training time*, propose and search for interpretable neurosymbolic multi-file policy repositories (*Repositories-as-Policies*) that compose these primitives rather than a single prompt, function, or file. RHO searches with reflective feedback from environment reward and execution rather than demonstrations. We show that our method generalizes to perturbed pick-and-place settings like LIBERO-PRO, reaching 64.33% success rate while CaP-Agent0, the prior leader, reaches 18.03% over the same primitive API, and VLAs trained from demonstrations, π₀.₅ and OpenVLA, achieve an average 13.20% and 0.0% success rate respectively. Under single-turn evaluations on Robosuite, RHO reaches 70.0% at 9.31 s per trial, exceeding the 68.29% prior record that required up to 6 turns of corrective LLM code edits and 113.6 s per trial, a 12.20× speedup. We further show that the RHO evolved repository also deploys unchanged to a different robot from that in simulation and successfully picks up objects never seen during training in 17 of 20 real trials. When an LLM is used in the control loop, as on RAI's hard O3DE benchmark, RHO optimizes the deployed agent's multi-file harness of prompts, tools, and control code, improving held-out success from 23.5% to 44.3% with 20% less wall-clock time and 27% fewer tool calls. Videos and further information: [https://rho-anon.github.io](https://rho-anon.github.io).

## Overview

**RHO moves interactive policy development from inference time to training time.** A coding agent uses robot execution feedback to develop, test, and refine multi-file repositories before deployment. In CaP-Bench, the selected repository runs as fixed code with no deployment-time LLM code generation.

### Benchmark APIs

CaP-Bench provides robot manipulation tasks in Robosuite and LIBERO. RAI connects an LLM agent to ROS 2 tools in the O3DE simulator. In both settings, a policy observes the scene and acts through the supplied APIs:

CaP-Bench exposes perception, grasp planning, inverse kinematics, and motion as separate calls. In RAI, `move_to_point` performs a fixed-orientation pick-and-place action using gripper commands and MoveIt motion planning and execution. The O3DE experiments expose the three tools shown above, with fixed names and signatures. RHO searches for repositories that compose the available APIs to maximize the evaluator’s score.

### Why search before deployment?

Multi-turn Code-as-Policies systems spend deployment time generating and correcting programs. RHO searches before deployment, preserving useful candidate repositories and refining them with execution feedback. In CaP-Bench it ships fixed policy code; in RAI it ships an improved harness around the existing LLM-driven loop.

### Kinova Gen3 with Robotiq gripper

We evaluated mouse lifting over 20 trials: 17 successes and 3 failures. We show selected trials at 1× speed, with the arm running at its configured speed.

Three things change between simulation and these trials.

 
 1
 A new object
 We ran the search on cubes, then deployed the repository to lift a computer mouse absent from simulation.
 
 
 2
 A moved position
 We moved the mouse between trials and, in one trial, during execution.
 
 
 3
 A different embodiment
 We searched with a simulated Franka Panda and deployed the same repository on a Kinova Gen3.
 

### Reading the failure

The arm descends three times onto the spot the mouse left. Grasp synthesis falls back to a path that places the grasp at the median of a segmentation mask's deprojected depth points, with orientation from a fixed top-down set. Those fall-back attempts stay anchored to the initial observation, so every retry targets a stale pose.

We found this by watching the trial, reading the logs and walking the code. We proposed a twelve-line repair that refreshes the object observation before a fallback retry, without retraining or new demonstrations. We have not tested this repair in these trials.
